_comment: What the release being prepared requires of an operator (ADR 0012, ADR 0013).
Authored by hand, like the CHANGELOG's Unreleased section; version and commit
are NOT here because they are derived at build time from the release identity.
`requires_operator_action` is derived too, from whether `actions` is empty -
NOTICES ARE NOT COUNTED, because a notice-only release is safe to take
unattended. See docs/self-hosting/release-manifest.md for the field reference.
_bootstrap: The bootstrap constraint is DISCHARGED: 0.1.0 shipped the guard declaring
nothing, as ADR 0013 requires of the first enforcing release - one that
refused traffic the moment it landed would punish installs already doing
the right thing. Later releases MAY declare actions.
_backups_queue_consumer: RESOLVED. This entry used to record why the backups-queue-worker
requirement was deliberately NOT declared, and the condition it named has
now been met, so it is declared - as a NOTICE.
The objection was never to the requirement, which is real, but to the
response available. The only phase it could have taken was `after-start`,
and an unmet after-start ACTION gates SERVING: an install missing a
backups worker would have refused all traffic, taking the whole support
platform down because a BACKUP worker was absent - on host-managed
installs only, since compose stacks start that worker themselves, whose
operator would then have to edit .env and restart with their site
already down.
ADR 0013 recorded the gap and named this requirement as the first
candidate for a third, non-blocking response. That response now exists:
`notices` is reported on the operator console, in wayfindr:upgrade-guard,
and in the installer's upgrade output, and the gates cannot see it.
So the response is now proportionate to the requirement, which is the
test that was always being applied - not whether the check existed.
It is verified by `check` rather than attested, so it retires itself the
moment a worker is actually seen; an operator who already runs one is
never told anything. It is also still reported where the operator meets
it - the backups page shows whether a worker has been seen - because the
person configuring backups should not have to read a release manifest.

_note: No `phase` and no `depends_on_release`: a notice never blocks, so
there is nothing to time and nothing to strand. Running a queue
worker needs no particular release's code, which is what makes
this legitimately advisory rather than an action in disguise.
`detail` DOES NOT print a copy-paste command, deliberately.
`BACKUP_QUEUE` can move the backups queue off its default, and a
manifest is static text - it cannot substitute this install's
configured queue or timeout. A hard-coded `--queue=backups` would
tell such an operator to start a worker draining a queue nothing
dispatches to, leaving backups queued forever after they did
exactly as they were told, with the check still reporting.
carries that warning, and the backups page builds the command from
the live config - so the notice names the requirement and points
at the surface that can get the command right.
notices.summary: Run a queue worker on the backups connection.
notices.detail: Without one, "Run a backup now" queues a job nothing will process and the run sits at Running indefinitely. Scheduled backups are unaffected. Compose stacks already run this worker. On a host-managed install, open /operator/settings/backups - it prints the exact command for this install, with your configured queue name and timeout filled in (BACKUP_QUEUE can move the queue off its default, so a copied command may drain the wrong one).
